newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Sky Aluminium sees loss erased by year-end.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Sky Aluminium sees loss erased by year-end.

text.p: Sky Aluminium Co, Japan's fourth largest maker of aluminium sheets, expects to eliminate its long-running accumulated loss by the end of 1996, said Sky's president and chief executive Kenichi Watanabe.

In a news conference on Wednesday announcing the privately held company's first-half earnings results, Watanabe said Sky held accumulated debt of 576 million yen as of the end of June 1996, down from 1.74 billion yen one year earlier.

Sky, whose principal shareholders are Showa Denko KK with 37.25 percent and Nippon Steel Corp with 36.25 percent, said its parent current profit in the half-year through June 1996 was 1.09 billion yen, off 10 percent from the same period last year, while its sales were up a marginal two percent year-on-year at 33.96 billion yen.

For the full year, Watanabe forecast sales at roughly double those of the first half and current profits at about 1.8 billion yen, with earnings expected to decline in the second half due to weak aluminium prices and stiff competition.
Sky's aluminium output in the first half totalled 79,000 tonnes, little changed from the previous year's 78,900 tonnes, while sales, at 77,900 tonnes, were up a marginal one percent.
Cool weather at the end of this summer, however, was expected to weigh on production and sales of beverage can sheets in the second half, Watanabe said.
He also said it was too early to predict when Sky may begin paying a dividend or go public, adding that the company wanted to strengthen its balance sheet before considering such moves.
He was also sceptical about indications of a pick-up in Japan's economy.
"That's only in the statistics," he said. "We don't have any real sense at all that the economy is improving."
He said he expected Japanese demand for aluminium, including exports, to show weak growth of about one or two percent in both 1996 and 1997.
He blamed sluggish growth in part on a slower-than-expected rise in demand from the automobile sector in recent years.
"We had hoped for more of a switch to aluminium in cars in the 1990s, but the pace has been slow," he said. -- Tokyo Commodities Desk (81-3 3432 6179)
